questions.stem: Which Article of the Constitution provides for the establishment of a High Court for each State?
questions.explanation: Article 214: 'There shall be a High Court for each State.' Article 124 deals with the Supreme Court. Article 226 grants HCs power to issue writs. Article 241 provides for HCs in Union Territories. Parliament can, under Article 231, establish a common HC for two or more states (e.g., Punjab & Haryana HC at Chandigarh).

questions.stem: What is the retirement age for a judge of the High Court in India?
questions.explanation: Article 217(1): HC judges retire at 62 years (originally 60; raised to 62 by the 15th Amendment, 1963). SUPREME COURT judges retire at 65 (Article 124). A key difference to remember: HC=62, SC=65. The CAG also retires at 65. These retirement ages are CONSTITUTIONAL and cannot be changed except by constitutional amendment.

questions.stem: Who appoints the Chief Justice of a High Court?

options.option_text: The Chief Minister of the State in consultation with the Governor
The President of India, in consultation with the CJI and the Governor
The Chief Justice of India alone, based on seniority

questions.explanation: Article 217(1): High Court judges (including the Chief Justice) are appointed by the PRESIDENT by warrant under his hand and seal, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, the Governor of the State, and (for other judges) the Chief Justice of that HC. Per the Second & Third Judges Cases (SC), the CJI's 'consultation' is effectively CONCURRENCE via the COLLEGIUM (CJI + 4 senior-most SC judges). The government proposed to replace this with the NJAC in 2014, but the SC struck down the NJAC Act in 2015.

questions.stem: Which of the following is NOT a type of writ that a High Court can issue under Article 226?
questions.explanation: Article 226 empowers HCs to issue FIVE types of writs: (1) HABEAS CORPUS — 'produce the body' (illegal detention); (2) MANDAMUS — 'we command' (direct public authority to perform duty); (3) PROHIBITION — prevent lower court/tribunal from exceeding jurisdiction; (4) CERTIORARI — quash lower court/tribunal order; (5) QUO WARRANTO — 'by what authority' (challenge a person's right to hold office). 'Summary judgment' is a civil-procedure concept (Order 37 CPC), NOT a constitutional writ.

questions.stem: Which of the following is the oldest High Court in India?
questions.explanation: CALCUTTA HIGH COURT was established on 2 July 1862 under the Indian High Courts Act 1861 — making it the oldest HC in India. Bombay HC was established on 14 August 1862 (same year, 6 weeks later). Madras HC on 15 August 1862. Allahabad HC came later (1866). These three — Calcutta, Bombay, Madras — are the original 'Chartered High Courts' of British India.

questions.stem: As of 2024, how many High Courts are there in India?
questions.explanation: India has 25 High Courts (as of 2024). The most recent additions: (1) Telangana HC separated from the common Andhra Pradesh HC in 2019; (2) common HC for Assam, Nagaland, Mizoram, and Arunachal Pradesh is the 'Gauhati HC' (so four NE states share one HC). Other groupings: Punjab & Haryana (at Chandigarh); HC of J&K and Ladakh (after 2019 reorganisation). The number ticks up as states split or reorganise.

questions.stem: The jurisdiction of a High Court under Article 226 to issue writs extends to:

options.option_text: To protect both Fundamental Rights AND for any other purpose
Only within the territorial boundaries of the State

questions.explanation: Article 226 is BROADER than Article 32 of the Supreme Court. While SC's writ jurisdiction under Art 32 is limited to enforcing FUNDAMENTAL RIGHTS, the HC under Art 226 can issue writs for: (1) enforcement of fundamental rights, AND (2) for any other purpose (e.g., statutory, common-law, or ordinary legal rights). This is why more cases go to HCs than directly to the SC under Art 32. HCs can also reach persons/authorities outside their territorial limits if the cause of action arose within.

questions.stem: Judges of a High Court can be transferred from one HC to another under which Article?
questions.explanation: Article 222(1): The PRESIDENT may, after consultation with the Chief Justice of India, TRANSFER a Judge from one High Court to any other High Court. In the Third Judges case (1998), the SC held that the CJI's opinion is based on the collegium's consensus, and the judge is entitled to a statement of reasons. A transferred judge retains his seniority but has to re-take oath in the new HC. Article 217 deals with APPOINTMENT.
